articles.title_zh: Cambridge Abandons Plans to Fully Investigate Its Hiring of Jason Arday

Published : Sep 24, 2026 20:17 IST  - 11  MINS  READ
A photo of late Cambridge professor Jason Arday, along with floral tributes, attached to the fencing by supporters around the Senate House at the University of Cambridge, in the town of Cambridge, eastern England, on August 18, 2026.
                                          | Photo Credit: Chris Radburn/AFP
Jason Arday was appointed professor of sociology of education at the University of Cambridge in February 2023, becoming, at 37, the youngest Black person ever appointed to a professorship at the university. The appointment was widely celebrated across British academia as evidence of institutional progress, in a sector where Black professors remain starkly underrepresented. In 2024-25, Black academics accounted for just 1 per cent of professors in UK higher education.
In July 2026, allegations of plagiarism, questions about his research and disputes over claims in his biography triggered a wave of media investigations into his work and public account of his life. Cambridge subsequently announced an investigation into his academic qualifications and honorary appointments, alongside existing complaints concerning academic misconduct. Arday resigned on August 5, days after the scrutiny intensified, saying his resignation should not be “mistaken for an acceptance of the narratives that have surrounded me”.
Nine days later, he was found unresponsive at his home in Battersea and pronounced dead, aged 41. An inquest subsequently opened after the coroner said there was reason to suspect an unnatural death. The inquest has been adjourned.
His case became a cultural battlefield over race, merit, diversity, representation and affirmative action. His exceptional visibility as Cambridge’s youngest Black professor was celebrated in British academia as evidence of institutional progress. At the same time, we need to think about how paradoxically intriguing his whole controversy was: the same visibility that was being celebrated made him disproportionately vulnerable to scrutiny and ideological attack.

There lies a substantial danger when institutions treat the presence of a marginalised individual as evidence that inequality has been overcome; representation might become a spectacle rather than transformation. Arday’s case asks for a rethink in the narrative of representation as inclusivity. There is a need to distinguish between representation as structural justice, when communities historically discriminated against demand the spaces they were never allowed to participate in, and representation as institutional tokenism, where a marginalised person is allowed to participate in an institution for the sake of inclusivity.
The excessive publicity surrounding his appointment itself illustrates a paradox: he was simultaneously recognised and othered. He was simply not allowed to be a scholar; he became a symbol of diversity, resilience, and institutional liberalism.
Many fail to see the underlying consequences such identity politics might produce and, in Arday’s case, the consequences explicitly came to the surface. It could be understood as “ghettoisation through representation”, where once an individual from a marginalised community becomes a symbol, their individuality is rendered secondary to the political function they perform for the institution. What happens when such individuals get to exercise their own agency within this contemporary diversity politics? Do they remain only as representatives of diversity? Identity politics cannot be dismissed altogether on account of such questions.
Asserting one’s identity through identity politics does not explicitly mean ghettoisation; in fact, identities which are “invisible” or have been historically invisibilised could utilise the very identity politics as a form of assertion. But the larger critique should ask whether mere institutional representation can be considered emancipation in itself. Do marginalised individuals still get to practise their agency via inclusive or diverse safeguards? Perhaps it’s intriguing to think that ghettoisation might not always occur through exclusion; sometimes, paradoxically, it occurs through inclusion itself.
Supporters take part in a vigil for late Cambridge professor Jason Arday in Trafalgar Square in central London on August 17, 2026.
                                                            | Photo Credit: 
                                Carlos Jasso/AFP
The Dalit scholar becomes the “Dalit academic”; the Black professor becomes the “Black success story”; the disabled student becomes an inspirational narrative. Their intellectual identity is constantly subordinated to their social identity. They are made hypervisible as members of a community but not recognised as autonomous intellectuals.
This produces a peculiar form of institutional violence. The privileged individual is allowed the luxury of being mediocre, complex, contradictory, or simply ordinary, but the marginalised individual must constantly justify their presence. Their failure is never merely individual; it is made representative of the supposed inadequacy of their entire community. Nobody would argue that the existence of a corrupt uppered-caste* professor proves that uppered castes are incapable of academic excellence, yet the failure of one reserved-category candidate is routinely mobilised as evidence against reservation itself. Such individuals, therefore, are denied the right to individual failure; they are simply not allowed the luxury of failure. Their failure is projected as an incapacity produced by the very communities they belong to. Affirmative action and representative politics carry this political violence within them, but the problem is not representation itself; it is the politics surrounding it, be it left wing or right wing.
The political Right attacks affirmative action through the language of meritocracy . It portrays reservation as an undeserved privilege and an assault on excellence. But this conception of merit deliberately forgets history: merit is never produced in a social vacuum. Who attends better schools? Who has educated parents? Who is surrounded by professional networks and intergenerational familiarity with universities? Such questions reveal who decides merit. Caste and racial privileges become invisible in the heap of merit.
This is where an Ambedkarite intervention becomes particularly necessary. B.R. Ambedkar , the anti-caste reformer and principal architect of India’s Constitution, demanded separate electorates for the Depressed Classes, the term then used for communities now broadly identified as Dalits. The British government’s Communal Award of 1932 granted separate electorates, but the Poona Pact of September 1932 replaced them with reserved seats within joint electorates.
It is crucial to understand that Ambedkar considered reservation a teleological tool, meaning a means directed towards a larger end, that would change the lives of Dalits in India, but he never considered it an emancipatory tool in itself.
Perhaps this is precisely why the same critique needs extending to the liberal Left. The political Left should not be treated as automatically emancipatory. Liberal and Left institutions often celebrate representation while refusing to transform their own internal structures. They celebrate the marginalised as evidence, or a token, of their own progress but grow uncomfortable when the same individual challenges their institutional power and hegemony.
Institutional discrimination does not simply vanish because a progressive Left politician comes to power. In India, we cannot forget the case of Chuni Kotal, an Adivasi woman of the Lodha community of West Bengal. articles.title_orig: U.S. Treasury yields tick higher as global bond rout slows
articles.title_zh: U.S. Treasury yields tick higher as global bond rout slows
articles.content_orig:
U.S. Treasury yields inched higher on Friday as recent selling pressure intensified following hawkish Fed commentary and stronger-than-expected economic data.
The benchmark 10-year Treasury note was up less than one basis point to 5.17%, after reaching its highest rate since June 2007 on Thursday. The 30-year Treasury bond was flat at 5.463%, after surging to levels not seen since 2004. The 2-year note yield was also little changed at 4.899%.
One basis point is equal to 0.01%, and yields and prices move in opposite directions.
Investors weighed a global bond selloff this week as Japanese government bonds, U.K. gilts, German bunds and other eurozone bonds hit fresh highs. Eurozone and Japanese government bond yields edged lower on Friday.
Treasury yields have been driven higher by hawkish comments from Federal Reserve Governor Michael Barr, who said in a speech on Wednesday that "further policy adjustments" can be expected to bring inflation down to target. Other factors included stubbornly high oil prices and the purchasing managers' index report hitting its highest level in more than four years.
Traders were last pricing in a nearly 71% chance of a rate hike in October, according to the CME FedWatch tool .
On Friday, investors will watch the University of Michigan consumer sentiment report and durable goods data.
"Ahead, we think that there are enough rate hike fears discounted at this juncture, and certainly enough to take care of perceived inflation risks," ING's regional head of research for the Americas Padhraic Garvey and senior rates strategist Benjamin Schroeder wrote in a note on Friday.
"But, government bond yields are primed to remain under pressure on a pure debt dynamic theory, which translates into pressure for some re-widening in swap spreads, and especially in the 10yr area."
"So far, Treasury Secretary Bessent's buyback programme has in fact been successful in the sense that it was followed up by tighter swap spreads."

articles.title_orig: Trump's state dinner for Xi features sea bass and a long list of tech titans
articles.title_zh: Trump's state dinner for Xi features sea bass and a long list of tech titans
articles.content_orig:
President Donald Trump shakes hands with China's President Xi Jinping in the East Room of the White House during a State Dinner, Thursday, Sept. 24, 2026, in Washington. Alex Brandon/AP hide caption
WASHINGTON — A tech-heavy guest list, the fashion choices of those on it, who sat where and what was on the menu marked the softer — often and glitzier — details of diplomacy as Donald Trump threw a Thursday night state dinner honoring China's leader Xi Jinping.
The event featured a cavalcade of billionaires, Washington powerbrokers, business leaders and the type of festivities that most excite Trump, who has a reputation for reveling in hosting parties.
"President Xi and I both understand we represent different systems, but the ties between our people endure, and we've never gotten along better," Trump said during his toast, adding that "together, we can continue to build a relationship that promotes prosperity and security for future generations."
Trump has done his best to impress Xi during China's leader's during Xi's three-day visit to Washington, and praised their close personal relationship — even as he has decried top Democratic candidates as "communists" ahead of the November midterm elections.
Xi and Trump discussed tensions over Taiwan, trade and artificial intelligence during business hours — even as an ongoing First Amendment fight over press access at the White House has unfolded. But Trump publicly chose to focus on showing Xi his White House updates on Thursday afternoon, including letting him tour his Marine One presidential helicopter and a new helipad he built for it — before attention quickly turned to the flashy details of the swanky meal.
Xi noted in his own toast that "President Trump has pledged to make America great again" and that "China is committed to achieving great national rejuvenation."
"These two goals are both ambitious and can surely be mutually reinforcing," Xi said.
President Donald Trump and first lady Melania Trump pose for a photo with China's President Xi Jinping and his wife Peng Liyuan in the Grand Foyer of the White House during a State Dinner, Thursday, Sept. 24, 2026, in Washington. Alex Brandon/AP hide caption
Trump wore a tuxedo, and her office said first lady Melania Trump opted for a tuxedo-style outfit: a white Saint Laurent cotton poplin blouse, a black silk cummerbund and black brocade pants — both from Dolce & Gabbana — with a peony motif.
Xi chose a black suit and his wife, Peng Liyuan, wore a red gown. The East Room, where the dinner was held, featured low lighting and place settings with elegant red and gold decor.
Those in attendance included OpenAI CEO Sam Altman, who signed autographs upon arriving at the White House. Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang opted for a tuxedo over his trademark black leather jacket. Bernard Arnault, the CEO of French luxury goods company LVMH, walked through black security fencing to enter the event.
The president toasted his strong relationship with Xi and the bond between the U.S. and China, but then added, "If I could go off script just for a second, I just want to say I had to do it," as those assembled laughed.
"I'd like to invite everyone in the room to visit through that beautiful curtain in the back," Trump said, referring to the construction site of his White House ballroom on the South Lawn, which he said, "you've heard so much about."
Trump said the project was a year from completion, and said he thought attendees "will see something that I think you will really love."
The president said that after the dinner attendees could go see the worksite and be "the first people to step foot" on it.
"We'll do that. Maybe after we've finished with the entertainment tonight," Trump said, asking, "Anybody wants to walk into a construction site that's nice and sparkling, it's our honor to have you do so."
Trump has called the ballroom he's building the "Great Hall of the United States," and suggested it could rival the Great Hall of the People, where he dined during a state visit to Beijing in May.
The president also presented Xi with an eagle statue that he said was designed "in personal collaboration with Melania and myself." Xi did not present Trump a public gift in return during the dinner.
The first lady helped craft the evening's menu, which was served on the red china from Ronald Reagan's presidency. It featured a first course of yellow squash velouté with wild mushrooms, fresh herbs, crispy pancetta and drizzled scallion oil.
The menu is seen at a seat as President Donald Trump hosts a State Dinner for China's President Xi Jinping in the East Room of the White House, Thursday, Sept. 24, 2026, in Washington. Alex Brandon/AP hide caption
After that, guests got sesame-crusted sea bass with braised baby bok choy, roasted garden eggplant and a sauce verte. Dessert was vanilla crémeux with sour cherry confit and walnut frangipane, as well as ice cream with honey from the White House.
The dinner came after the president took the unusual step of personally greeting Xi and his wife on Wednesday as they arrived at Joint Base Andrews outside Washington. Normally, presidents wait for their state visit guests to arrive at the White House itself before offering a formal welcome.
Thursday's dinner was packed with technology industry titans like Amazon founder Jeff Bezos, Tesla and SpaceX CEO Elon Musk, Google and Alphabet CEO Sundar Pichai, OpenAI President and co-founder Greg Brockman, and Dell Technologies chairman and CEO Michael Dell.
During his own visit to Beijing in May, Xi hosted Trump for a state dinner that unfolded beneath grand chandeliers in the Great Hall of the People. That event also included many tech luminaries, such as Tim Cook, formerly Apple's CEO, and Musk.
It was all a stark departure from 2015, when then-President Barack Obama was preparing to host Xi for a state visit and Trump — in the midst of his first presidential run — criticized all the hubbub.
"Just take them to McDonald's and go back to the negotiating table," Trump said then, during a rally in South Carolina. He later conceded on Fox News Channel that Xi might at least be worthy of getting "probably a double-size Big Mac."

articles.title_zh: New Jersey Gov. Sherrill calls on her lieutenant governor to resign
articles.content_orig:
Mikie Sherrill says Dale Caldwell ‘engaged in serious, repeated violations’ involving staffers and gifts
New Jersey’s governor on Thursday called on the state’s lieutenant governor, Dale Caldwell, to resign by Friday after a law firm hired by her office concluded he violated the state’s ethics and discrimination rules.
The report published Wednesday found that Caldwell violated the state’s policy prohibiting discrimination in the workplace. It said he made an advance toward a staffer’s friend and when he was rebuffed, he told the staffer: “You young women are looking for young sperm.”
“The investigation found that the Lieutenant Governor engaged in serious, repeated violations of state policy and failed to uphold the responsibilities of his office,” Mikie Sherrill, the governor, said in a statement.
Caldwell’s lawyer, Thomas Calcagni, disputed the allegations, calling the investigation a one-sided operation that did not include necessary due process.
“The Lieutenant Governor was not provided a meaningful opportunity to address each of these anonymous allegations,” he said in a statement.
The report also accused Caldwell of breaking the state’s ethics rules by trying to get a promotion for a state employee he was dating and by bringing his personal guests to ticketed events without paying for them.
“Where a sponsor waives admission to an event for an official’s family member, friend, or date, the value of that admission is an impermissible benefit to the official,” the report said.
Sherrill, a Democrat, said Caldwell’s “ethical lapses” continued even with multiple warnings and trainings. She called his resignation “in the best interest of New Jersey residents”.
“These violations substantiated in the investigation reflect a pattern of behavior that does not meet the standards of this Administration,” she said.

articles.title_orig: Bob Pettit, basketball great who was named the NBA’s first MVP, dies at 93
articles.title_zh: Bob Pettit, basketball great who was named the NBA’s first MVP, dies at 93
articles.content_orig:
Bob Pettit, an imposing scorer and rebounder for the St. Louis Hawks and winner of the NBA's first Most Valuable Player award in 1956, has died. He was 93.
Pettit's alma mater, LSU, announced Thursday that he died a day earlier. The university did not provide a cause of death.
Pettit was an All-American at LSU before going on to the NBA, where he was an All-Star for each of his 11 seasons, all with the Hawks. He led them to the 1958 championship over the mighty Boston Celtics, the Hawks' lone title.
He was also the NBA MVP in 1959 and was the MVP of the All-Star Game four times, an achievement matched only by Los Angeles Lakers great Kobe Bryant.
Pettit was a force at a time when the NBA featured the likes of Wilt Chamberlain, Bill Russell, Oscar Robertson and Elgin Baylor. But it was also before a time when the NBA was widely seen on television, and Pettit — playing in a smaller market — was denied a larger audience.
At 6-foot-9 and 205 pounds and with a deeply receding hairline, Pettit was a physical presence at power forward, before such a position became part of basketball's vocabulary. He rarely missed a game. He also played center and was one of the first big men who did not play solely with his back to the basket.
Pettit was the Rookie of the Year in 1955, the last year the Hawks played in Milwaukee before moving to St. Louis.
He captured the MVP the next season, leading the league in scoring at 25.7 points a game. He also was the NBA's scoring leader in 1959 at 29.2 points.
He retired after the 1964-65 season with career averages of 26.4 points and 16.2 rebounds. At that time, he was the NBA's career leader in points (20,880) and second in rebounds (12,849).
He was inducted into the Naismith Memorial Basketball Hall of Fame in 1970.
"Lean, graceful, and always well-conditioned, Bob Pettit's physical build made him one of the first big men to play facing the basket," reads Pettit's biographical profile at the Hall of Fame. "But Pettit's resolve set him apart from his peers; he simply would not be outworked."
Robert Lee Pettit Jr. was born on Dec. 12, 1932, in Baton Rouge, Louisiana. His father worked in law enforcement and served as East Baton Rouge Parish sheriff. Pettit was a late bloomer in basketball, not making the Baton Rouge High School varsity until his junior season.
As a senior, he led Baton Rouge to a state championship and wound up with more than a dozen college offers. He chose to stay home and starred at LSU as a sophomore, an era when players could not join the varsity until then.
He led the Southeastern Conference in scoring all three of his seasons, with averages of 25.5 points as a sophomore, 24.9 as a junior and 31.4 as a senior.
Pettit is one of only three LSU players — Pete Maravich and Shaquille O'Neal the others — to earn a place in the Hall of Fame. Bronze statues of Pettit and O'Neal stand outside LSU's home arena, the Pete Maravich Assembly Center. His No. 50 is retired by LSU, his No. 9 by the Atlanta Hawks.
Pettit's misfortune was that most of his career coincided with a run of Celtics championships that remains one of the most dominant runs in American pro sports history.
Pettit was two victories short of being a three-time NBA champion. Pettit's Hawks advanced to the finals four times, all against Boston, twice losing in seven games.
The first meeting, won by Boston in 1957, came down to double overtime of Game 7. The second ended with a championship for the Hawks, interrupting Boston's run of nine titles in 10 seasons. The Hawks also dropped NBA Finals matchups with the Celtics in 1960 (in seven games) and 1961 (in five).
Pettit retired to his native Baton Rouge after leaving basketball and worked in banking and financial consulting. He was a regular at LSU and New Orleans Pelicans games in recent years.

With António Guterres ’s nearly decade-long tenure as the Secretary-General of the United Nations drawing to a close amid rising conflict around the globe, the race to succeed him as the leader of the world’s most powerful diplomatic body is already underway.
Guterres this week delivered his final address to the U.N. General Assembly , in which he called for a greater focus on climate change, a two-state solution for Israel and Palestine, “de-escalation and dialogue” in the Middle East, and regulations for artificial intelligence.
At the end of his speech, Guterres bid goodbye to a crowd filled with many diplomats and world leaders who he has worked with over his two five-year terms.
"So, on January 1st, when ​I am no longer Secretary-General, be sure of this. Wherever I will be, whatever I will be doing, I will keep championing the conviction that peace is possible," he said. "I will continue ​to stand up for the values of the United Nations Charter and I will never, ever give up. Thank you."
Guterres’s successor is set to step in as Secretary-General at a consequential moment for global diplomacy. Research indicates that last year saw the highest number of active global conflicts since World War II and the greatest number of fatalities since the Rwandan genocide. Tensions in other parts of the world are threatening to boil over. Climate change is exacting a growing toll . AI's development is prompting increasing alarm . And the U.N. itself is confronting a growing funding crisis.
Read More: Make the U.N. Great Again: The Uphill Struggle Facing the Next Secretary General
Seven candidates are so far in the running to shepherd the U.N. through those challenges. Here’s what to know about the race.
The process to choose the next Secretary-General began in November, when a joint letter from the presidents of the U.N. General Assembly and Security Council invited the nominations of candidates from member states.
The initiation letter noted “with regret that no woman has ever held the position” and encouraged member states to “strongly consider nominating women as candidates.”
Member states nominate candidates by submitting an application to the U.N. including a personal statement with that candidate’s vision for what they’d do in the role, a resume, and campaign finance disclosures.
The General Assembly then holds “interactive dialogues” in which candidates express their hopes for the position and the U.N. in an opening statement, which is followed by questioning from the assembly. These televised hearings continue as candidates are submitted to the U.N.
Who becomes Secretary-General ultimately comes down to a decision from the U.N.’s 15-person Security Council, which recommends one individual to the General Assembly. The General Assembly then appoints that person to the position.
As part of its selection process, the Security Council holds “ straw polls ,” in which members of the council select one of three options for each candidate: “encourage,” “discourage,” or “no opinion expressed.” This anonymized process is used to gauge whether candidates would be able to secure the nine votes needed for a formal recommendation by the Security Council.
So far nine candidates have been nominated for the position of Secretary-General. Two of those candidates have withdrawn, leaving seven individuals vying to replace Guterres.
Carolyn Rodrigues Birkett has been Guyana’s permanent representative to the U.N. since 2020 and previously served as foreign minister for her country and held senior roles at the U.N. Food and Agriculture Organization. Nominated by Guyana, her vision statement emphasizes refocusing on the U.N.’s core principles and “a more agile and effective United Nations.”
Rebeca Grynspan is the former vice president of Costa Rica, which nominated her for the position, and current secretary-general of trade and development for the U.N. She named three principles that define the mission she would undertake as Secretary-General: making the U.N. “more useful,” “more agile,” and “more accountable.”
Ivonne A-Baki, nominated by Tonga, is a long-time Ecuadorean diplomat who has twice served as the country’s ambassador to the U.S. She has also served as ambassador to countries including Qatar and France. Her platform highlights her involvement in the 1998 Ecuador-Peru peace settlement. “Where others speak of reform, I speak of renewal,” A-Baki’s vision statement reads. “An institution can be indispensable and in need of renewal at the same time, and ours is both. It is failing to live up to its own Charter, not for want of purpose but for want of focus and discipline.”
María Fernanda Espinosa is the former Foreign Minister and Defense Minister of Ecuador and served as President of the 73rd U.N. General Assembly in 2018. She was nominated by Antigua and Barbuda. Her vision consists of five pillars: “peace and security, development, digital and energy transformation, closing the delivery gap, and rebuilding credibility.” Garcés in her statement contended that “what is now in question is not the relevance of the United Nations, but its credibility.”
Rafael Mariano Grossi is an Argentine diplomat who has served as the Director General of the International Atomic Energy Agency (IAEA) since 2019. “The world does not need more declarations. It needs a United Nations capable of responding to the real demands of our time, with impartiality and a results-oriented approach grounded in facts,” Grossi, who was nominated by his country, wrote in his vision statement.
Olara Otunnu was Uganda’s permanent representative to the U.N. for five years and briefly served as the country’s foreign minister. He was also the U.N. under-secretary-general and the special representative for children and armed conflict. “Reform is no longer an optional choice. It is an imperative,” he said .
Macky Sall was the president of Senegal for twelve years and has served as the chair of the Africa Union, a continental organization spanning 55 member states. He expressed a goal to “restore trust in multilateralism” if chosen as Secretary-General and said that “peace, security and development are intrinsically linked.”
“We're at a moment right now where the race is entering a pretty pivotal phase,” says Daniel Forti, head of U.N. affairs at the International Crisis Group, a non-profit think tank dedicated to preventing deadly crises around the world.
With just over three months remaining in Guterre’s term, it won’t be long before a successor is chosen. The Security Council, though, “is not especially enthusiastic about any of the current contenders,” Forti tells TIME. He cites the last three straw polls, which have favored Greenspan and Birkett, but without “a real consolidation of overwhelming support.”
This lack of consensus, Forti believes, could suggest that other candidates may enter the race late in the game. Although there have been no formal announcements of new candidates, Forti has heard chatter surrounding certain individuals: Nickolay Mladenov, the former Bulgarian foreign minister and former U.N. Middle East envoy who currently serves as the Board of Peace’s High Representative for Gaza; U.N. Deputy Secretary-General Amina Mohammed; and former Mexican Foreign Minister Alicia Bárcena.

Trump likely shrugged off Pezeshkian UN attack as he 'holds the cards,' foreign policy expert says.
Iranian President Masoud Pezeshkian’s sharp rebuke of Washington at the United Nations would have drawn little more than a "smirk" from President Donald Trump, who knows he "holds the cards," a foreign policy expert told Fox News Digital Wednesday.
The assessment came after Pezeshkian and Trump addressed the U.N. General Assembly in New York from the same podium within 24 hours of one another, trading sharp rhetoric as tensions between Washington and Tehran continue to mount.
"Trump understands he holds the cards, and he may not even have paid much attention to what the Iranian president was saying," Behnam Ben Taleblu , a senior fellow at the Foundation for Defense of Democracies (FDD), told Fox News Digital.
Pezeshkian accused the United States and Israel of attacking Iran while portraying his country as the victim of aggression.
THE TOP MOMENTS FROM IRAN PRESIDENT’S TENSE VISIT TO US SOIL AS WAR RAGES
Iranian President Masoud Pezeshkian holds a picture, which he says is from the Minab school that was hit by an airstrike, as he addresses the 81st session of the United Nations General Assembly at U.N. headquarters Sept. 23, 2026, in New York City. (Spencer Platt/Getty Images)
"We have only defended ourselves. We are not terrorists," Pezeshkian claimed.
"Our innocent people have been the targets of cowardly attacks and aggressions imposed upon our country. America and Israel attacked us."
"I’m sure that would have drawn a smirk or a smile or a chuckle from the president’s face, seeing that crassness," Taleblu said, pointing to what he described as a sharp contrast between Pezeshkian’s rhetoric and the Iranian government’s track record.
Pezeshkian’s address came after Trump used the same U.N. stage to defend the U.S. conflict with Iran and warn that Tehran faces a stark choice between reaching a deal and facing further destruction.
"Or do I annihilate the Islamic Republic, and do it quickly, never giving them a chance to kill and destroy people and countries again?" Trump said on Tuesday.
While the rhetoric from both leaders was pointed, Taleblu said their broader diplomatic positions remain largely predictable.
TRUMP TO ZERO-IN ON IRAN NUCLEAR THREAT, GAZA PLAN AND UN OVERHAUL IN WORLD STAGE SPEECH
President Donald Trump addresses the UNGA in New York City. (Michael Santiago/Getty Images)
"To a certain degree, both President Trump and President Pezeshkian’s speeches before the U.N. General Assembly’s 81st session were predictable," Taleblu said.
"Predictable because the status of both countries and their foreign policy toward the other are in a fairly predictable pattern right now."
Despite the threats and recriminations, the two adversaries also appear to be still testing a diplomatic path behind the scenes.
Trump said Tuesday that U.S. special envoy Steve Witkoff and Jared Kushner spoke with Iranian officials for roughly three hours on the sidelines of the General Assembly and characterized the discussions as productive.
Witkoff later said the talks were conducted through mediators who shuttled between the U.S. and Iranian delegations.
Iranian Foreign Minister Abbas Araghchi also represented Tehran in the discussions, according to reports.
KUSHNER TOUTS UNPRECEDENTED IRAN CONTACTS AS TEHRAN DENIES TRUMP BACKCHANNEL
Iranian President Masoud Pezeshkian and President Donald Trump (Majid Saeedi/Getty Images; Jose Luis Magana/AP)
Both sides, Taleblu said, are attempting "to make time a weapon on their side" and "to put the burden of choosing between escalation and engagement on the other."
But Taleblu went on to characterize Pezeshkian’s broader message as an attempt to cast Iran as a victim through an anti-American, anti-Israel and anti-imperialist framework.
"It seemed to be more of a global South, anti-American, anti-Israeli, kind of anti-colonial, anti-imperialist message that he was looking to kind of paint the Islamic Republic as the victim," Taleblu said.
"In reality, the long-serving victim in this entire crisis is the Iranian people because of the policies of the Islamic Republic."
The competing messages — confrontation from the U.N. podium and diplomacy behind the scenes — highlighted the unresolved tensions between Washington and Tehran as officials explore whether negotiations can produce an off-ramp from the conflict.
TRUMP KEEPS FORECASTING AN IRAN DEAL — WHY THE WHITE HOUSE STILL THINKS IT CAN HAPPEN
Iranian President Masoud Pezeshkian addresses the 81st session of the United Nations General Assembly at U.N. Headquarters Sept. 23, 2026, in New York City. (Alexi J. Rosenfeld/Getty Images)
"Despite the tough talk at the podium, both sides still feel like they need to signal an interest in talks, even though they’re both trying to use talks to shape an outcome that is more conducive to their interests," Taleblu said.
Pezeshkian also told the General Assembly that Tehran would not surrender to military pressure while signaling that Iran remained open to diplomacy .
"I think the Iranians are trying to signal an interest in talks, but they may run into a brick wall quite soon if they foot-drag or delay or don’t meaningfully provide any kind of substantive change in their policy," Taleblu said, citing Iran’s positions on the Persian Gulf, the Strait of Hormuz and its nuclear program.
"Ultimately, if the positions remain the same, the fact that they’re oscillating between shooting and talking doesn’t mean much because the red lines haven’t actually moved.

articles.title_orig: Meloni government bans burqas, caps foreign students in Italian schools
articles.title_zh: Meloni government bans burqas, caps foreign students in Italian schools
articles.content_orig:
Italy’s government has moved forward with plans to ban face coverings in schools and cap the number of foreign students in classrooms. It has also threatened to exact fines of up to $1,140 for breaches of the new rules.
Prime Minister Giorgia Meloni outlined the proposed changes on Sunday at a gathering of the youth wing of her nationalist conservative Brothers of Italy (FdI) party. On Thursday, Meloni’s cabinet adopted the decree-law, rendering the wearing of burqas and niqabs in schools illegal and introducing a 30-percent cap on non-Italian speakers in classrooms starting next year.
Failure to comply will be punishable with a fine of up to $1,140 (1,000 euros).
The measure is a decree-law, meaning it can take effect immediately, but it must be ratified by parliament within 60 days.
President Sergio Mattarella, who also has to sign off on it, flagged this week that he was wary of any barriers being placed on education.
Meloni said the “tools” to learn the Italian language and “stop” burqas and niqabs in schools were “common sense that do not divide” in a post on her X account.
“This is the direction we want to continue to follow: a school that integrates without giving up on rules, that supports those who have more difficulties and that puts everyone in a position to start from the same point,” she wrote.
Opponents said the government was using the rules to try to counter the growing appeal of the far-right National Future (FN) party led by former army general Roberto Vannacci ahead of next year’s elections.
FN, which has made schools a central battleground in its campaign advocating “remigration”, called for a crackdown on burqas in schools in July.
Opposition politicians accused Meloni of prioritising culture-war politics over the interests of students and schools.
“It is a shameful decree that seeks to hide the government’s inability to address the real problems of the public school system behind a new ideological banner,” Elly Schlein, the leader of the centre-left Democratic Party, said.
Education Minister Giuseppe Valditara said local school authorities will coordinate student placements to avoid concentrations of non-Italian-speaking pupils, while schools unable to comply would be eligible for exemptions and additional language-support funding.
He said it would affect about 1,000 classrooms, or about 0.3 percent of the total nationwide.
Teachers’ unions criticised what they called a lack of both consultation and resources for the measure.
School principals questioned how the measure could work in areas with large migrant populations.
“From an educational perspective, the issue is well-founded and valid, but it’s difficult to turn it into a practical solution,” Antonello Giannelli, president of the National Association of Principals, said.
According to Education Ministry data, non-citizen students accounted for 11.2 percent of Italy’s school population in the 2022-23 academic year, while classes with more than 30 percent foreign students represented 7.6 percent of the total.

Republicans are increasingly breaking from President Donald Trump over the war in Iran .
A growing number of GOP candidates are calling for an end to the nearly seven-month-long war on the campaign trail, even in traditionally red parts of the U.S. On Capitol Hill, the latest war powers resolution weighed by the House was approved with fresh Republican support. And recent polls show that as the conflict has stretched on and hit Americans’ wallets , approval of Trump’s handling of the war among Republican voters has dropped by double digits.
The defections come as active hostilities in Iran have resumed in the last month after peace talks between Washington and Tehran stalled over the summer. Trump, who initially projected that the war would last a matter of weeks, has in recent days publicly floated the possibility that he could “ annihilate the Islamic Republic ” and “ blow the entire nation up .”
At the same time, however, he has also recently predicted that the conflict will end after the midterms . And not long after levying a fresh threat in his speech before the United Nations General Assembly, he told reporters at the diplomatic gathering that he had a “very good” meeting with “mediators of Iran.”
“It's to their advantage to make a deal, and we can do that,” he said on Tuesday.
Still, lawmakers on both sides of the aisle have voiced concern that Trump has not laid out an exit strategy for the conflict and sounded alarm about the impact the war is having on fuel prices , which have spiked around the U.S. since it began.
With GOP fears over the pivotal November elections growing, more candidates and lawmakers in the party are choosing to distance themselves from the President on the issue—and though the defectors remain in the minority, Republican strategists tell TIME that GOP disapproval for the war in Iran will likely only continue to mount.
A handful of Republican candidates have recently pushed for an end to Iran on the campaign trail as the midterms near, including several in tight Senate races.
“It's all about getting reelected,” Brian Darling, a Republican strategist and former counsel to Sen. Rand Paul of Kentucky, says about midterm candidates to TIME. “It's all about making sure that they can signal to their constituents that they have the same concerns about the Iran war."
Darling asserts that much of the discontent over the war in Iran stems from its inflationary impact within the U.S. A Congressional Budget Office report released last week found that the war has driven up energy prices in the U.S. mainly due to disruptions to shipments through the Strait of Hormuz, a vital shipping route through which one fifth of the world’s crude oil flows, adding 2.3 percentage points to the annualized rate of inflation of 5.3% in the second quarter of 2026. The price of regular gasoline is up around 52% from the start of the war at around $4.48 per gallon, according to the U.S. Energy Information Administration, with diesel prices up 71% in the same period.
Read More: U.S. Diesel Prices Just Surpassed a Record $6 Per Gallon. Here Are Three Ways That Affects You
For many Americans, these rising prices are among the most important issues when voting in the midterms. A Reuters/Ipsos poll from late August showed that 47% of voters said the cost of living would be the single most important factor for them when deciding who to vote for in November.
On top of that, support for the war is low, with only a quarter of Americans believing that it’s worthwhile, according to the same poll. And though Republicans still back the conflict in greater shares than Democratic and independent voters, surveys show that their sentiments toward it have notably soured in the months since it began. A YouGov poll conducted between Sept. 18 and 21 found that a slim majority of 53% of Republicans say that in hindsight going to war in Iran was the right decision, a drop of 15 percentage points from the 68% that said the same in April. Another recent poll conducted for CNN by SSRS found that Republican approval of the war fell from 73% in March to 60% in the latest survey period of Sept. 16-17. Among Republicans under the age of 45, 53% disapproved of the war. Republican fears that the party could lose control of Congress in the midterms have meanwhile been on the rise, fueled by election forecasters shifting key battleground states and districts toward Democrats in their ratings and polls indicating that voters favor Democratic congressional candidates on generic ballots.
“The bottom line for most candidates is they want to talk about the Iran war and ending the Iran war as a solution to our high gas prices,” Darling says.
Candidates calling for an end to the Iran war have explicitly pointed to its effect on prices in their remarks.
“Iowans are being squeezed and shouldn’t have to foot the bill at the pump or the checkout line for the war in Iran,” Rep. Ashley Hinson, the GOP nominee for Senate in Iowa, posted on X on Monday, saying that “the war needs to be brought to a successful and immediate end.”
Former Rep. Mike Rogers of Michigan, who is also running for Senate in his state, made his own call for ending the war in an ad this week in which was shown standing in a grocery store.
“The war with Iran needs to end, and end quickly,” he said, referencing ballooning gas and food costs. “Michigan families are struggling with the price of everyday life. Groceries cost too much. We have to bring prices down.”
“The war needs to come to an end as quickly as possible so that we can lower gas prices,” Sen. Jon Husted of Ohio, who is facing a tight race to retain his seat this year, similarly told POLITICO in an interview published on Tuesday.
Trump has previously dismissed concerns about the war’s impact on gas prices, which he has called “ a very inexpensive price to pay for what we’ve done ” and “ peanuts .” But on Tuesday, while speaking alongside Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelensky at the U.N. General Assembly, he said that his Administration is considering banning diesel exports to quell the increase in fuel prices.
Read More: What a Diesel Export Ban Would Mean for U.S. Consumers
“I’ve called for that, too. I said, ‘Let’s not send out the diesel.’ We make a lot of diesel. I’ve called for it—I’ve called for it with my people,” Trump said.
Although Darling holds that inflation is the main source of voters’ disapproval toward the war in Iran, he contends that many GOP lawmakers and voters are also fed up with U.S. involvement in armed conflict in the Middle East and around the world.
“You have some Republicans who are anti-interventionists, and some who are realists, and look at the situation in Iran and just don't see an end game,” Darling says, making reference to the U.S.’s involvement in Afghanistan and Iraq, which he said voters look to with fear as a “very similar circumstance” to Iran.
Trump, who campaigned on vows to put “America first” and not to get the U.S. involved in new foreign wars , has drawn backlash from his base for his military interventions in Iran, and in other parts of the world .

articles.title_orig: Iran offers US new seven-day ceasefire proposal
articles.title_zh: Iran offers US new seven-day ceasefire proposal
articles.content_orig:
Country says US must lift sanctions on its oil exports and end the war on all fronts, including in Lebanon
Iran said it has told Donald Trump it is willing to open the strait of Hormuz in six days, and to start talks on its nuclear program the day after, so long as the US lifts sanctions on Iran’s oil exports in return, ends the war on all fronts – including in Lebanon – and releases some of Iran’s frozen assets.
The proposal is designed to accelerate the steps first laid down in the memorandum of understanding signed by the US and Iran in June, particularly by helping the talks on Iran’s nuclear program start much more quickly than previously agreed.
Iran says a deal on the temporary route through the strait of Hormuz has been agreed with Oman, describing it as a done deal, and is ready to register the details with the International Maritime Organisation.
Abbas Araghchi, the Iranian foreign minister, said he was waiting to hear a response from the Americans to the proposal. He added that he had consulted on the plan with China, which fully supported the proposal.
Saudi Arabia had been expected to endorse the Oman-Iran route through the strait last week, but pulled back partly due to anger that Iranian-backed Houthis had started attacking Saudi Arabia as part of their dispute over the future of Yemen.
Iran claims it has urged the Houthis to cease the attacks on Saudi Arabia but that it does not have control over Houthi decision-making.
Araghchi, speaking to reporters in New York, said: “We have introduced a plan to the US through the mediators that if certain conditions are met, the strait will be open within seven days and talks will start.”
He said the Iranian preconditions were not new, and were contained in the Islamabad memorandum of understanding that was signed by Trump.
The advantage of the proposal, apart from opening the strait and lifting the chokehold on the world economy, would be bringing the US to the talks on Iran’s nuclear program much more quickly. Talks on the nuclear program under the MoU would not have started for 60 days. Araghchi said he was staying in New York over the weekend to await an American response, but added he was not in a hurry.
Privately, Iranian officials believe they could reach a deal with the Americans, and the Saudi hurdle over aspects of the route could be overcome, but fear Israel will use its influence to pull the US president away from the proposal.
Araghchi added he would like the deal to go through before the midterm elections, by which he meant that the strait of Hormuz could be opened and energy prices thereby reduced, something Trump badly needs for the Republican party to survive a political mauling.
For the US, there are difficulties in the plan related to forcing Israel to end the war in Lebanon. Israel may object to giving Iran such clear control over the route through which ships would travel through the strait of Hormuz. Iran also wants to retain control of shipping to prevent some US military shipping going through the strait.
Issues such as whether tolls or navigational fees could be imposed by the littoral states Oman and Iran would be settled later in the process.
Earlier in the day, the UK foreign secretary, Ed Miliband , met Araghchi, his Iranian counterpart, for the first time in New York.
It was also the first meeting between UK and Iranian ministers for a year, and the first exchange since the UK in July proscribed the Islamic Revolutionary Guards Corps (IRGC) as a terrorist organisation, a move that has worsened the already sour relations between the two countries.
Miliband made clear that the UK was committed to freedom of navigation in the strait and wanted a diplomatic solution, also stressing support for Saudi Arabia, a UK ally in Yemen.
He warned Iran about its behaviour in the UK, including threats to Jewish communities, and called for the UK to be given consular access to the British couple sentenced to 10 years’ imprisonment in Tehran.
Araghchi and the US’s special envoy Steve Witkoff also met earlier this week on the sidelines of the general assembly to discuss Iran’s terms for reopening the strait and the speed at which that may happen, as well as the time the US had been given to respond.
A faction inside Iran is arguing that Tehran should seek to escalate the conflict with a vulnerable US president, rather than let the crisis drift in its current deadlock. Brent crude was trading at about $107 (£81) a barrel on Thursday.
Some IRGC officers have also linked the strait of Hormuz issue to the closure of the Bab al-Mandab strait, the narrow waterway close to the south-west of Yemen now under control of Iranian-backed Houthis.
Maj Gen Rahim Safavi, a senior Iranian military figure, said: “If the Americans start a new war, a new front centred on the Red Sea and the Bab al-Mandab strait may open before their eyes. Are they ready to enter the battle on this front? This is a question that they should pay more attention to.”
Domestically, Pezeshkian’s defiant message to the UN general assembly on Wednesday was deemed a success overall in that it balanced a refusal to bend the knee to “the US bully” with a willingness to seek diplomatic talks.
He also proposed a new security architecture for the future in partnership with Gulf states, including those it has been bombarding in an effort to dislodge the US from its military bases.
Maj Gen Ahmad Vahidi, commander-in-chief of the IRGC, praised Pezeshkian’s speech, saying: “We are not afraid of war. It is the loud and firm call of the Iranian nation – a call that resonated from the United Nations podium, through the words of the esteemed president, and reached the ears of the world.”

articles.content_orig:
Oracle shares fell more than 3% on Thursday following news that the company sent a "force majeure" notice tied to its New Mexico data center project to protect itself from higher expenses.
"Project Jupiter remains on our planned schedule," Oracle said in a statement to CNBC. "We are fully committed to New Mexico and confident in our path forward."
Bloomberg was first to report the news, citing sources familiar with the matter.
The company is looking to delay payment on the campus, dubbed Project Jupiter, if it fails to come online as expected in 2028, according to the report.
Oracle sent the notice to the developer, which is a unit of Blue Owl Capital , CNBC confirmed. Blue Owl also saw its shares fall on Thursday.
"This notice does not change the financial commitments to this multi-year project," Blue Owl Capital said in a statement to CNBC.
The New Mexico data center project, which is part of the broader Stargate artificial intelligence infrastructure build-out with President Donald Trump , has been riddled with setbacks and regulatory hurdles.
That includes local opposition to data centers ahead of the upcoming midterm elections and concerns from environmental groups. The site has also faced delays with the buildout of a natural gas pipeline intended to fuel the facility.
Shares of Bloom Energy, which is slated to power the more than 2.4-gigawatt facility with its fuel cells, fell 3% on the news. In a post to X, the company said it remains "committed" to the contract and following the "planned timeline."
Oracle co-CEO Clay Magouyrk told analysts on the company's earnings call on Sept. 10 that Project Jupiter would not affect its previously stated fiscal 2027 revenue or earnings guidance.
Concerns have also mounted over Oracle's $18 billion in debt tied to the data center, which is already trading at stressed levels, according to the Financial Times.
— CNBC's Seema Mody and Leslie Picker contributed reporting.

articles.content_orig:
By REBECCA LAWRENCE, DEPUTY SHOWBUSINESS EDITOR (DIGITAL FEATURES)
Published: 03:16 EDT, 25 September 2026 | Updated: 03:56 EDT, 25 September 2026
She's famed for documenting her romantic woes through her music.
And while this year may have been the one that Taylor Swift finally settled down and tied the knot with Travis Kelce , fans are convinced that she was reminiscing about a past relationship in her latest single.
The billionaire popstar, 36, dropped four new songs on Friday with the release of The Life Of A Showgirl: The Encore, an extended edition of her 2025 album.
Four new songs are included in the release - Patient Zero, Pink Clouding, Babylon and Cleveland! - with the final song seemingly a reference to her new husband's hometown of Ohio .
However, fans are convinced that Patient Zero - a single about a toxic former relationship - is about her romance with Joe Alwyn .
The couple dated for six years from 2017 until early 2023, in what was Taylor's longest, and arguably most low-key, relationship to date. There were rumours of an engagement, but neither Joe nor Taylor publicly confirmed the reports.
Taylor Swift fans are convinced Patient Zero is about Joe Alwyn after she released a new song about a toxic relationship. They dated for six years before splitting in 2023 (pictured in 2020)
The billionaire popstar, 36, dropped four new songs on Friday with the release of The Life Of A Showgirl: The Encore, an extended edition of her 2025 album
Now fans believe she's documented their romance in Patient Zero which saw Taylor seemingly sing about a social-climbing ex.
The single has similarities to her 2022 track, You’re Losing Me - widely believed to be about Joe - which referenced medical terminology, while Patient Zero has a pulse sound in the background.
You're Losing Me has the lyrics 'Stop (Stop, stop), you’re losing me / I can’t find a pulse, my heart won’t start anymore', which echo Patient Zero's 'When the toxins take their hold / You’d rather die than let it go.'
Patient Zero also has similarities to another track believed to be about Joe - 2019's Cruel Summer - in which she referred to him as 'grinnin’ like a devil.'
In Patient Zero, she sings about 'the devil on his shoulder under his halo.'
Other lyrics from her new single reference an ex stepping into the spotlight after dating her - with English actor Joe relatively unknown outside the UK before their romance.
She sings: 'I bet he burst into your life like fireworks/I bet he even said "I love you" first/And when you saw another woman coming out of his place/I bet he kissed the rain of your face.
'I know he charmed your family and friends/And you thought it's 'cause he loves you/But it's 'cause he loves how everybody loves him.

California's state Supreme Court ruled Thursday that a Republican sheriff must hand back more than half a million ballots he confiscated for an inquiry into unsubstantiated claims of voter fraud during a special election last year.
Riverside County Sheriff Chad Bianco in February seized roughly 650,000 ballots from a November 2025 special election regarding statewide congressional redistricting that favored Democrats and was championed by Gov. Gavin Newsom. The measure comfortably passed across the state and won in Bianco's county by about 80,000 votes.
Calling the seizure "unlawful," the court stated that California law mandates voted ballots remain under the custody and control of election officials, even during a criminal investigation. Bianco must also "refrain from further handling of the ballots except as necessary to comply with our order," the court ruled unanimously. Bianco did not immediately comment on the ruling.
"If election misconduct is suspected, the Elections Code provides several mechanisms for law enforcement to review and examine ballots without compromising their integrity," the court wrote.
Bianco’s ballot inquiry occurred as President Donald Trump has repeatedly disputed the results of the 2020 election, citing unsubstantiated instances of fraud. His administration in January seized ballots and other documents from an election office in Georgia, with some Republicans adopting similar voting rhetoric in their states.
Election authorities and civil rights organizations have followed the Bianco case closely as they prepare for the possibility that Trump or his allies might try to seize ballots in November.
Bianco stated that he confiscated the election materials as part of a criminal investigation following a complaint from a local citizens group claiming the tally was incorrect. Local election officials had previously determined the complaint was unfounded. Bianco was running for governor at the time, but he failed to advance past the primary.
Democratic Attorney General Rob Bonta immediately filed a legal suit, arguing the sheriff possessed no authority over election records and warning that the seizure was designed to sow distrust in elections. He ordered Bianco to return the ballots, but the sheriff refused.
"The Court has now made clear that this kind of defiance cannot stand, that the Attorney General has the authority to intervene when sheriffs take improper action, and that voted ballots belong in the custody of elections officials," Bonta said Thursday.
The University of California, Los Angeles Voting Rights Project also filed suit against the sheriff and the Riverside County Registrar of Voters on behalf of several Riverside County voters. The state Supreme Court heard arguments in both cases last month.
The Court also established that obtaining a search warrant does not override state election law.
"The Court’s decision reaffirms a basic principle that in California, the Election Code applies to everyone, including law enforcement," said Chad Dunn, legal director and co-founder of the UCLA Voting Rights Project. "These are the voters’ ballots. They must be protected through the processes the Legislature has established. This ruling provides important clarity for election officials, law enforcement, and voters across California."
Newsom on Saturday signed legislation that prevents anyone from seizing ballots in the manner Bianco did.
Shortly after seizing the ballots, Bianco began recounting the vote using sheriff’s officials under the supervision of a court-appointed special master, but he suspended the effort days later amid mounting legal challenges from the state attorney general and the voting rights group. However, he has not returned the ballots.
Bradley Hertz, representing Bianco before the court, argued the sheriff was under a legal duty to launch a criminal inquiry after receiving a complaint and followed the penal code by issuing search warrants in February.
Hertz said Bianco has not returned the ballots to the Riverside County Registrar of Voters because those materials are "evidence."
When the ballots were seized, Bianco was one of two prominent Republicans competing for governor in a crowded June primary. He did not reach the general election and later announced plans to run for reelection as sheriff in 2028.
Xavier Becerra, a former state attorney general and Democrat currently running for governor, is part of the UCLA lawsuit seeking to halt Bianco’s efforts.

articles.title_orig: Presidents Cup: Scottie Scheffler, Sam Burns sneak through tough opening round as U.S. takes early lead at Medinah
articles.title_zh: Presidents Cup: Scottie Scheffler, Sam Burns sneak through tough opening round as U.S. takes early lead at Medinah
articles.content_orig:
Nobody can legitimately question how good of a golfer Scottie Scheffler is. He's the top-ranked golfer in the world for a reason, and has absolutely dominated the PGA Tour over the last several years.
But Scheffler's struggles on the international stage, a trend he can't seem to shake, continued on Thursday at Medinah Country Club in Chicago.
Scheffler was in the opening group at the 2026 Presidents Cup on Thursday, playing alongside Sam Burns in the first of five four-ball matches against the International team. The two managed to sneak out a 1-up win over Min Woo Lee and Sungjae Im, thanks to a huge save at the 17th, to get the United States on the board. It was also the first Presidents Cup or Ryder Cup match that Burns and Scheffler have won playing together.
By the end of the day, the U.S. took a 3-2 lead over the International team ahead of the foursomes matches on Friday. They've led after the opening session in 12 of the 16 Presidents Cups.
"We just did our best to stay in it," Scheffler said. "I felt like both teams got off to pretty hot starts today and we cooled off a little bit off that."
Scheffler opened the day with a walk-in birdie. But that was about his only highlight. Lee and Im quickly tied the match back up as Scheffler struggled to get much of anything going. He missed the green at the short par-3 7th and hit his tee shot into the crowd, for example, and couldn't get many putts to fall the rest of the way.
That largely left Burns as the one to try and hold things down. He sank a big birdie putt at the 9th to keep the match tied as they made the turn, and Lee and Im missed three straight birdie looks of their own that would have given them their first lead of the day. They finally jumped ahead of Burns and Scheffler on the 13th after Scheffler missed a 3-footer for birdie, though Burns made a putt on the 14th to even things up once again.
Scheffler got a 4-foot par putt to fall on the 17th, while Im missed a similar look in a rough mistake, to finally put the Americans in the lead for good. Scheffler had to save par after landing in the bunker at the 18th, however, to avoid splitting the point.
Scheffler's record on the international stage is lagging behind his other accomplishments. He's got a 3-6-3 record at the Ryder Cup, and he entered this week with a 3-5-1 record in Presidents Cup matches. Scheffler has never won a Presidents Cup singles match, either, though he's 2-0-1 in those at the Ryder Cup.
Scheffler and Burns, who are very good friends off the course, were a combined 0-3-1 when paired together at the Ryder Cup and Presidents Cup before Thursday's win. Not great.
Luckily for Scheffler and the Americans, they're now in the lead after the first day in Chicago. Just not by much.
"I saw those guys competing their asses off out there," U.S. captain Brandt Snedeker said. "I'm really proud of them. A session win is a session win, we're going to take it any way we can get it. So happy for Scottie and Sam to go out there in that lead match and get that big win for us to lead us off.
"This is a long week. This is one session. We've got four more to go. Just proud of the way these guys started us off."
While the Scheffler-Burns group was slow, two pairs of Americans wasted no time in their matches behind them.
Justin Thomas and rookie Jackson Koivun rolled to a 4&3 win over Corey Conners and Nico Echavarria in the third match of the day. Koivun made three birdies on the front side to grab a lead almost immediately, and Koivun — who only made his PGA Tour debut mid-season earlier this year — looked comfortable out there.
Thomas then sank a birdie putt of his own from off the green at the 14th to push their lead back to three, which was enough to carry them to the early win. Thomas has now won his last seven four-ball matches at the Presidents Cup, which is tied for the all-time record. And at 21, Koivun is now the second-youngest American behind only Jordan Spieth to win a Presidents Cup match.
Wyndham Clark and Collin Morikawa cruised to a similar 3&2 win over Ryan Fox and Adam Scott. Clark went 4-under on the front nine himself, which was more than enough to keep Fox and Scott at bay. Clark then pushed their lead to three with a birdie on the 15th, which allowed them to end the match on the following hole.
Scott is playing in his 12th career Presidents Cup, and Thursday was his 55th overall match, both of which tied the all-time record with Phil Mickelson.
While they were in the last and slowest group of the day, Tom Kim and Si Woo Kim had little issue getting past Chris Gotterup and Patrick Cantlay, winning 3&2 to secure an easy point for the Internationals.
They went 2-up through their first two holes to take control of the match almost instantly. While Cantlay and Gotterup rallied briefly — they made three birdies in a four-hole stretch to tie things up — that was all they could do. Cantlay became a non-factor the rest of the way while Kim and Kim easily pushed their lead to three before taking the win. Si Woo's birdie at the 14th was from distance, too, and banked in perfectly.
Tom nearly had a hole-in-one at the 16th and actually banked his ball off the flag stick. That would have been the third ace in Presidents Cup history.
Hideki Matsuyama and Ryo Hisatsune, meanwhile, took off on the back nine to grab their 3&1 win. After hanging in a battle on the front nine, the pair won back-to-back holes before making the turn to take control of the match while Xander Schauffele and Cameron Young struggled to get putts to fall. Eventually, after Young missed a birdie look at the 17th, Matsuyama and Hisatsune were able to put the Internationals on the board for the first time all day.
The two teams will return to Medinah on Friday for five foursomes, or alternate shot, matches.

articles.title_orig: 'Primetime' examines 'To Catch a Predator' through a ghoulish lens
articles.title_zh: 'Primetime' examines 'To Catch a Predator' through a ghoulish lens
articles.content_orig:
Robert Pattinson, one of the great on-screen chameleons of his generation, plays Chris Hansen with a nervy slickness that brushes up against madness, writes Hertz. A24/Supplied
Directed by Lance Oppenheim
Starring Robert Pattinson, Merritt Wever and Skyler Gisondo
Classification 14A; 110 minutes
Opens in theatres Sept. 25
Is it possible to feel good about getting sick to your stomach? That is one of the many queasy questions viewers of the excellent but nauseating new satirical thriller Primetime will be compelled to contemplate as director Lance Oppenheim and his star Robert Pattinson take you on a guided tour of humanity’s very worst instincts, in which all roads lead to a kind of sweeps-week hell that rivals Dante’s Inferno for divinely sick comedy.
In Primetime ’s underworld, Virgil is personified by Chris Hansen, the real-life NBC journalist whose vigilante-tinged series, To Catch a Predator, marked an inflection point for trash TV and American pop culture writ large.
Airing from 2004 through 2007, the reality show set up a series of sting operations in which adult actors enlisted by the so-called watchdog group Perverted Justice impersonated underage boys and girls in online chat rooms. After the phony teens enticed, or perhaps entrapped, men to come over to their homes for sex, Hansen and his camera crew would suddenly emerge from the shadows to confront and interrogate the would-be pedophiles, the “gotcha” moment quickly followed by the arrival of police officers.
‘This goes way beyond Chris Hansen’: How Primetime’s Lance Oppenheim turned the tables on trash TV
It was all lurid, sordid material that unwittingly revealed Western culture’s own inherent perversions – of justice, of punishment, of pleasure – and in Primetime acts as the fuel for a truly bracing and audacious cinematic nightmare.
Pattinson, one of the great on-screen chameleons of his generation – and an actor who is currently enjoying a historic big-screen run this year between this movie, The Odyssey , The Drama and the forthcoming Dune: Part Three – plays Hansen with a nervy slickness that brushes up against madness. Aping Hansen’s gentle but confrontational voice with creepy perfection, Pattinson plays the journalist as a man of sweaty and epic desperation, part media-circus carnival barker and part tortured freak of the week. It is the performance of the year, demanding recognition.
In Oppenheim and Pattinson’s admittedly over-dramatized, deliberately garish version of Hansen’s vortex of a life and career, the man is portrayed as an abject failure of a father (his wife, briefly played by Anna Faris, cannot stand him) and a reporter (he views Stone Phillips as his arch rival, even if that NBC newsman doesn’t much think of him at all). Hansen isn’t even that much of a moral crusader, either, given that at the same time he is busy setting up traps for potential rapists, he’s also skirting the queries of a National Inquirer reporter who is looking into his own extramarital affair.
Tony Revolori and Robert Pattinson in Primetime. A24/Supplied
Yet Primetime doesn’t limit its perspective to Hansen alone, with Oppenheim carefully expanding the story’s scope to include a host of opportunists and suckers, predators and prey. There is Dan Plumb, a composite character based on a handful of aspiring young actors who worked on Hansen’s show impersonating young teens. As played with sweet but quickly curdling innocence by the wonderful Skyler Gisondo, Plumb begins the film as a naive performer eager for an easy paycheque, but quickly starts to realize that the opportunity of a lifetime comes with a high cost. Meanwhile, the entire operation is overseen by Andie Bender, a cutthroat television producer played by Merritt Wever, who imbues the character with grit and wit.
Even the bit characters have range, with Oppenheim assembling one of the best-cast films of the year. The too rarely seen Bokeem Woodbine is tremendously intimidating as a Texas police chief with hate in his heart and assault rifles in his trunk. Musician Phoebe Bridgers is haunting as Plumb’s female counterpart, who more immediately recognizes the damage she’s doing.
A handful of exceptional character actors – Tony Revolori, Alex Winter and one-time Jerry Maguire child star Jonathan Lipnicki – take bold, gigantic risks by daring to give a sliver of humanity to the comically long parade of pathetic, sick men lured in to To Catch a Predator ’s web. And Oppenheim even gets an astounding, bordering-on-evil-genius performance from former NBC executive Jeff Zucker, who plays a heightened version of himself with a distinct, terrifying lack of irony.
As Hansen pushes his show to become more intense and extreme – as if he needs the shock value of what happens on screen to jolt his own soul from slipping away into the void – Oppenheim similarly amps up the film’s visual excesses. Gradually, the movie becomes greasier and sleazier, its images oversaturated and its editing off-kilter. Just as you might bristle and twitch uneasily at stumbling upon an episode of To Catch a Predator today, the more that Primetime unspools, the more dangerous and wrong it begins to feel.
While Oppenheim never underlines it in the way that a filmmaker with more bluntly obvious tactics as, say, Oliver Stone might, a direct line can be traced from the backwards righteousness of To Catch a Predator through to our current, deeply hypocritical Make America Great Again era. What is the difference, in the end, between Hansen’s fear-mongering shtick and the child-trafficking conspiracies of Pizzagate and other QAnon-led delusions, enraging fantasies that are egged on by the architects of the American right as cover for the very real crimes of sitting politicians and power brokers?
Primetime is not an easy film, but it is an essential one. Do not adjust your sets.

articles.title_orig: US mortgage rates top 7% for first time in 20 months
articles.title_zh: US mortgage rates top 7% for first time in 20 months
articles.content_orig:
Increase comes after Fed decision to raise interest rates, as Americans struggle with high prices and stagnant wages
US mortgage rates surpassed 7% for the first time since January 2025, according to federal lender Freddie Mac, aggravating a housing market that has endured years of high interest rates and low supply.
The increase comes after the US Federal Reserve hiked interest rates , which directly affect mortgage rates, for the first time since 2023, citing high inflation.
Rates on 16 September went up by a quarter of a point, to a range of 3.75% to 4%. In new projections, a majority of the Fed’s rate-setting committee predicted at least one additional rate hike before the end of this year.
Last year, the Freddie Mac 30-year-mortgage rate, commonly used on home loans across the country, had been trending down from 7.79% – a generational high reached in late 2023.
But rates have been creeping back up since late February, when the US and Israel launched its war with Iran . The conflict drove inflation to its highest levels in three years and sharply increased energy prices.
Brent crude, the international benchmark for oil, topped $105 earlier on Thursday.
after newsletter promotion
On Thursday, the 10-year US treasury yield – which underpins the 30-year mortgage rate and other borrowing costs – also reached its highest level since July 2007 and the 30-year Treasury yield hitting its peak since 2004 as investors raised expectations for another Fed rate hike next month.
Earlier in September, US treasury secretary Scott Bessent announced the Treasury would triple its buyback of government debt, but yields have continued to rise.
The housing market has long been in a slowdown, said Anthony Smith, a senior economist at Realtor.com , with existing home sales hitting their 2026 low so far in August and pending sales that have turned negative year over year.
“A 7% handle is as much psychological as mathematical, and it arrives at the point in the season when leverage usually shifts toward buyers,” said Smith.
High mortgage rates are just one of the many reasons why Americans are struggling to attain home ownership. Wages have not kept pace with higher inflation, and everyday costs are higher.
The frustration is expected to show up in November’s midterm elections as Republicans struggle to maintain control of Congress. Nearly three-quarters of Americans disapprove of Donald Trump’s handling of the economy, according to a recent CNN poll conducted by SSRS , and two-thirds of registered voters rate the economy as “extremely important” to their vote.

articles.title_zh: University of Mississippi identifies 2 students found dead in cases that raise kratom concerns
articles.content_orig:
The University of Mississippi said Thursday that undergraduate students from Colorado and Georgia died this week in cases that sparked renewed concerns about kratom .
Aidan Hamilton, 18, a freshman from Englewood, Colorado, and Robert Strang, 20, a junior from Atlanta, were found dead in separate locations this week, Ole Miss said.
Both students were discovered Monday, one on campus and the other in the city of Oxford, authorities have said. Packaged kratom was found during each of the death investigations, but no definitive link has been made between kratom and the deaths, officials said.
Kratom is an herb with opioidlike effects sometimes sold at gas stations or online. It has gained popularity in the U.S. as an unapproved treatment for pain, anxiety and drug dependence. Kratom can be stimulating or sedating, depending on the dosage taken, according to the Drug Enforcement Administration .
“We are heartbroken by the loss of our dear son, Robert, and are trying to process this unimaginable loss,” the Strang family said in a statement. “We are deeply grateful for the incredible outpouring of love, prayers and support by so many beloved friends and family. Their kindness has meant more to our family than we can ever express.”
“As we grieve and focus on our family, we ask for privacy, understanding and compassion in the days ahead,” the statement said.
The Hamilton family said Aidan Hamilton was “a bright, wonderful young man who was taken too soon.”
“He is greatly missed. We thank everyone for their prayers and support and ask that you respect our family’s privacy during this time of great loss,” the family said in a statement.
Shawnboda Mead, the university’s vice chancellor for student affairs, cautioned the campus community about misinformation.
“We know there is heightened media attention and that you may be eager for answers. We also recognize that inaccurate information is being shared by individuals who do not have access to the facts,” Mead said in a statement .
“We can all help by not repeating information that has not been officially confirmed and by avoiding public speculation about what happened or why, especially as the causes of the two deaths are still under investigation.”
Phi Delta Theta fraternity said Strang was a member.
“Out of respect for Robert, his family, and those closest to him, the Fraternity has refrained from public comment until his name was publicly released,” it said in a statement Thursday.
“The loss of two young lives is a profound tragedy,” it said. “Phi Delta Theta joins the University of Mississippi and the broader Ole Miss community in mourning Robert and Aidan Hamilton and extending our deepest sympathies to their families, friends, chapter brothers, classmates, and all those who knew and loved them.”

Games must be “fully usable with hands, end-to-end,” Meta says, noting that Touch controller support is welcome, but not required.
“For a small team without a marketing budget, that visibility drives traffic to your Store listing and gives you something concrete to point to when you pitch a new project or recruit collaborators,” Meta says.
This comes ahead of the company’s Meta VR Glasses announced at Connect this week, which does support Quest’s Touch Plus controllers, but doesn’t ship with them, instead putting its onboard hand and eye-tracking as its preferred control scheme.
Those are set to arrive sometime in Spring 2027, priced at $1,300. Check out our hands-on with Meta VR Glasses to learn more .
The competition takes place from today until November 18th, 2026, and is offering up prizes ranging in value from $20,000 to $100,000 for successful submissions. Winners will be announced on or around December 11th, 2026.
Since Meta VR Glasses run the same operating system as Quest, developers can prototype on Quest 3 in addition to using platform simulators like Meta XR Simulator ( Unity | Unreal ), Meta Spatial Simulator , and Immersive Web Emulator⁠ .
Interested developers can join the Start program now to enter for competition.
